beta_new: From below the E side of the formation, work up a series of zig-zagging ledges to the summit; a short 4th-class perfect hand-crack section is one of the standard variations.

moves.from: Little to no protection is typically placed.

beta_new: From a high parking area on FR6517 about 0.5 mile east of the summit, the route gains about 1,460 ft in all, finishing with roughly 600 vertical feet of open slope/talus to the top — easy class 2 if you stay to the right side, or class 2/3 up the center. Total distance is well under a mile each way, and the round trip from the car is typically under three hours. The peak sees very few visitors compared to nearby Beckler Peak and Evergreen Mountain.

The standard route follows the Bean Creek Trail from the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead up the Bean Creek drainage to Earl Pass, then climbs the southwest ridge on intermittent tread to the summit. It is rated class 2 in dry summer conditions but is also a popular spring snow scramble that can require an ice axe and crampons on the steep, icy south-facing summit slopes.

From a trailhead off Standup Creek Road, follow the Standup Creek Trail (#1369) up an old roadbed, crossing Standup Creek six to seven times (the first crossing is the largest; later ones range from brushy to easy rock-hops), passing wildflower meadows and a small waterfall, then switchbacking through forest to reach a ~6,200-ft saddle shared with the Bean Creek Trail approach — about 3,200 ft of gain over roughly 4.5 miles. From there the route joins the same open ridge crest used by the Southwest Ridge for the final ~0.7 mile / 900 ft scramble to the summit, described by longtime climbers as non-technical except a short step onto the summit block.

Traverse right from start toward the large hanging 'split block'. Pitch 1 offers a 5.8 finger crack or easier ground to its right, and pitch 2 has a critical 25-30 foot unprotectable section on a dyke. Pitch 3 climbs through a chimney and dirty corner. The final pitch offers laid-back climbing in an obvious corner approach to summit, though the final moves to the horned summit are unprotectable. The route requires careful rock quality assessment and awareness of unprotected sections.

From high camp, ascend moraine to the Chimney Glacier, cross the bergschrund via snow/ice blocks, then scramble exposed 4th-class ledges to the Main Notch between the South and Main peaks. From the notch, a 3rd/4th-class 'reddish ramp' and further scrambling lead to a broad ledge below the summit tower, where climbers rack up for 3 roped pitches to the top. Rock is generally sound but has loose ('choss') sections; many parties note the bergschrund/moat crossing is often the technical crux of the day, not the rock pitches.

Established over 3 days in September 2008 by Alan Kearney and Erik Johnson (a route Kearney had attempted in 1991 and 2003), the line follows the peak's northeast buttress up compact gneiss with few natural crack systems. The pair placed small cams and numerous knifeblade and bugaboo pitons for protection and drilled no bolts; the route is described as featuring dark, brooding overhangs, a delicate traverse, sections of blank rock, and loose, teetering blocks near the top.

Roughly three-quarters of parties climb Snowking via this East/Kindy Ridge line, the least technically demanding of the mountain's four recognized routes (the others being the Northwest Route, West Route, and Illabot Creek Route). From an overnight camp near Cyclone Lake or higher on the ridge, follow heather benches and easy slabs up the ridge crest, staying near the crest and side-hilling around minor gendarmes and cliff bands where the ridge is blocked — the route's technical crux, rated around Class 3. The final few hundred feet climb easy snow/scree below the summit block, staying off the Snowking Glacier proper, before a Class 3 scramble tops out from the south/SSE side.

From the Cedar Creek Trailhead, gain the ridge early and follow its crest essentially the whole way to the summit, passing several sub-summits along the way. Route-finding on loose rock is the main challenge; difficulty rises to 5.9+ V or harder if a party ropes up earlier or maintains continuous contact with the ridge crest.

The East Ridge begins with a bergschrund crossing and several pitches (mostly 5.7, often simul-climbed) up vegetated ledges and blocky rock to gain the ridge crest and east face. A 5.8 pitch leads into the route's signature crux: a sustained hand/fist crack (5.9) that nearly every trip report singles out. Above the crux, moderate 4th/low-5th-class climbing continues along an exposed, knife-edged crest to the true summit. The route is graded III, 6 pitches, 800 ft, but many parties describe the full outing — including simul-climbed sections — as feeling more like 8-10 pitches / Grade IV given the long glacier approach and multi-rappel descent.

Considered the easiest way up Mount Thomson and the standard descent for the West Ridge as well. After the long PCT approach to Bumblebee Pass and down into the basin, a steep heather-and-talus slope gains an obvious notch (~5,600 ft) on the peak's ESE ridge; from there the route trends left across class 3 terrain to a short, exposed 20-ft class 4 step guarding the true summit, which most parties protect with a rope.

From the Castle-Pinnacle col, take the obvious east ridge up Pinnacle. Pitch 1 scrambles mostly 4th-class terrain to a belay ledge at a large dead tree. Pitch 2 is the crux: blocky mid-5th-class climbing with an exposed traverse (an old, unreliable piton is present) to a sandy belay bench that has a fixed rappel anchor dropping the south face. Pitch 3 is mellow terrain to the true summit and is often simul-climbed or soloed by comfortable parties. Loose rock and scree are a serious, persistent concern throughout.

Little more than a walk once the Lucky Pass col is reached — the difficulty of this route lies almost entirely in the approach (creek crossing, steep brushy ridge gain, and a glacier traverse), not the summit scramble itself. Most parties treat it as a 2-3 day backcountry trip out of Colonial Creek Campground.

The South Route climbs East Twin Needle from Crescent Creek Basin by the loose south-facing gullies to the Eye Col, the notch between East and West Twin Needle. Small chockstones low in the gully are scrambled past; the larger ones higher up are fifth class and are usually pitched, and a short scree walk finishes at the col. From the col the route climbs the steep summit block directly above, with a short hand-crack crux near the top that can hold ice early in the season; the summit is small, with a sheer drop to the east. This is a different climb from the hard southeast ridge/face (east arête) put up during the 2003 Southern Pickets enchainment, which is reached along the crest from the east and is not gained from the Eye Col.

moves.from: Descend by downclimbing and rappelling back to the Eye Col, then down the south gullies with several short rappels off natural anchors.

beta_new: Climbed via the historic 1945 Beckey-Staley line on the spire's southeast side: from the east notch, a short pitch gains a ramp system that is followed up and west, then a final slab/crack pitch (crux) leads to a summit ledge. The rock is loose in places (especially early in a pitch or on the east aspect), so care with hand/footholds and rope management is important on this wandering line.

moves.from: Two short raps and a downclimb return to the notch.

beta_new: Stellar rock quality with excellent crack and corner climbing plus slab sections; because of the demanding approach, parties typically have the route to themselves. Use 'Zebra Corner' as the key landmark throughout the climb to confirm you're on route - it can seep water early season. Blake Herrington's Cascades Rock topo is the recommended reference since the wall has more variations than are documented online.

From the Eldorado Creek trailhead, a steep boot trail gains a talus basin near 4,000 ft; open slopes lead to a high camp between roughly 5,400 and 7,800 ft near the Eldorado Glacier margin. From camp, rope up and cross the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers, gain 'the Gap' on the lower East Ridge, then follow the exposed snow crest to the small summit.

Approach via the East Ridge glacier track to a rappel notch between Eldorado Peak and Dean's Spire (~8,100 ft), rappel into the west-facing cirque, then climb the couloir (~1,000 ft, 7,800–8,800 ft) on snow, neve, or ice depending on conditions — steps to 70–80° — to join the upper East Ridge.

From high camp, descend the Inspiration Glacier to the notch used as the NW Ice Couloir rappel point, then climb steep snow onto the North Ridge proper. The route follows generally solid rock on the ridge's eastern aspect with good friction and incut holds, offering minimal exposure toward the glacier side but dramatic exposure to the west. Near the top, parties can finish directly up steeper ice/rock or join the classic East Ridge finish to the summit.

First climbed in 1969, the West Arete follows the crest of Eldorado's west face for about 19 pitches (including 3 long simul pitches). The lower section is loose 5.6 scrambling through a steep open chimney; the middle section has confusing routefinding through sandy, loose gullies (5.0-5.7) with relentless exposure; the crux is a set of rocky towers finishing in an old-school 5.8 face traverse protected by a single in-situ piton; the upper section continues with chimney climbing and more 5.0-5.7 pitches before three long, loose simul pitches lead to the summit. Most parties treat it as a full multi-day outing: a day to approach, a long day to climb (historically up to ~17 hours round-trip from the East Ridge base camp), and a day to exit.

From the Diablo trailhead, the maintained Sourdough Mountain Trail is followed to about 4,300-4,400 ft before leaving the trail on an unmarked climber's path to reach the open crest of Sourdough/Stetattle Ridge. From there it's an extended, largely trail-less ridge walk (with a short class 3 step near a saddle) toward Elephant Butte. The peak itself presents an obstacle: a short overhung 5th-class move goes more or less directly over it (not recommended with an overnight pack), while most parties instead drop well off the ridge and traverse below/around the peak through brush and mossy micro-cliffs before regaining the ridge crest beyond it. Most climbers do this as part of a multi-day traverse into or out of the Southern Pickets rather than as a dedicated objective, though a very long single-day round trip from Diablo is feasible for fit, fast parties.

Named for the daughter, Ella, of one of the first ascensionists. Pitch 1 is a bolted groove; pitches 2-3 mix flakes, thin cracks, seams, and steep friction (the mental crux); pitches 4-7 climb knobby, well-bolted face and corner terrain up to sustained 5.10; pitch 8 finishes on a steep juggy face into a flaring corner at 5.11a (or 5.10 with a point of aid). Protection mixes bolts with natural gear throughout — most pitches are partially bolted.

A ground-up effort by two Spokane climbers over several days across a few seasons, completed in 2009. Excellent, squeaky-clean granite throughout, with a well-bolted crux pitch of pocket climbing and a steep exit from the cave regarded by many parties as the route's hardest pitch. The large Supercave itself offers a natural mid-route rest/shelter.

This is the generic 'easiest route' taken by nearly every party that visits Emerald Peak, almost always as a side-summit from a basin camp shared with Cardinal and/or Saska Peak. It is described consistently as: gain a basin around 6,800-6,900 ft below the Cardinal-Emerald saddle, cross talus/scree to the base of a broad gully, climb the gully (moderate snow early season, loose scree/rock later) to a notch in the summit ridge, then turn and scramble class 2-3 rock (only a very short stretch of class 3 near the top) to the summit. This line has no formal name; 'Southeast Ridge' describes the ridge/notch it gains relative to Cardinal Peak, which sits just SE of Emerald.

Despite the peak's craggy appearance suggesting no easy line exists, erosion has cut a class 3 gully/weakness up the west side that is catalogued as a named, rated route (skill 2 / fitness 2). It tops out on a summit divided into two high points roughly 100 ft apart — the north summit is slightly higher, and the south summit has notably more exposure, with a steep slab dropping toward the East Face.

moves.from: Access is via the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 from the standard trailhead, or alternately via the Emerald Park Trail #1230 starting from Lucerne on Lake Chelan's shore (a boat-access approach).

beta_new: Peak order and exact lines are up to the party; the loop below runs west to east. Stuart: from the Stuart Lake valley climb slopes toward Long Pass, then steep snow to a notch at about 7,950 ft on the northwest face; drop slightly, traverse snow to a gully that shortcuts onto the upper West Ridge (continuous snow early season, with 3rd class rock beside it), then follow the West Ridge to the summit. The West Ridge is a notorious route-finding trap that benights parties climbing it for the first time, so know the line before you go. Sherpa: descend the upper Cascadian Couloir and cut east to the Stuart-Sherpa col (a short 4th class downclimb on the way), then climb Sherpa's West Ridge, keeping left of the steeper cracks on easier ground. Leave Sherpa by the north side: a short 4th/5th class downclimb, then trend skier's left through a scrambly gully to a large vegetated ledge near 8,100 ft, and on down a broader gully to about 7,200 ft. Sherpa to Argonaut: a long, time-consuming traverse across high granite slabs and goat paths to Argonaut's south-side gullies; the alternative is to drop to the valley trail and climb back up. Argonaut: ascend the southern gullies on easy ground to just below the east ridge, with a short easy-fifth-class step to the summit; descend by rappel down the east face. Colchuck and Dragontail: gain the Colchuck-Dragontail col and tag each summit by its scramble from the col, then descend to Aasgard Pass. The Core: from Aasgard Pass continue into the upper Enchantment basin for Little Annapurna (a walk-up from the basin), McClellan Peak (loose scrambling), then Enchantment Peak via Prusik Pass (talus, with a 4th class summit pillar; it has two summits of similar height, so tag both if in doubt) and finally Cannon Mountain from the Enchantment side.

From a camp in the Core Enchantment Zone, or straight off Aasgard Pass on a long day, cross the lakes basin and leave it between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun, heading north over talus to the gully on the south side directly below the northeast summit. The going is class 2-3 with a few exposed spots and good holds, and a short third-class scramble up the south side finishes on the northeast summit, a flat block about 6 ft square and the true high point. The southwest summit, roughly 1,500 ft away along the crest, is a narrow, very exposed fourth-class (some say low fifth) fin and is not part of this route; the Prusik Pass east-ridge route is the other way onto the northeast summit.
Starts on water-polished rock, pulls a small roof, works through a thin crux, then hangs on through a leftward traverse on good holds to the bolted anchors.

From the trailhead, cross the North Fork Teanaway River and follow talus and snow slopes up to the base of the gully on the east side of the East Peak. The lower gully starts as debris-covered Class 2-3 scrambling, then steepens into Class 4 climbing on poor holds with a trickle of water running down the rock. After roughly 500 ft the gully becomes steep, loose, essentially unprotectable, and wet; most parties exit via a short chimney on climber's right to traverse around this section at low 5th-class difficulty before a horn where a side gully rejoins the main line. Above this the climbing eases somewhat but the rock remains loose ('Cascade ball bearings'), continuing to a final ridge walk to the East Peak summit.

From the De Roux trailhead (3,800 ft), follow the Boulder-De Roux Trail #1392 roughly 3 miles west up the valley between Esmeralda Peaks and Koppen Mountain, passing several waterfalls, to a scree field near the final switchback (~5,600 ft) marked by a house-sized boulder. Leave the trail here and climb straight up a sustained, ~1,100 ft Class 2 scree/talus slope to the west summit (6,776 ft, true high point and register location); many topo maps mark the eastern summit (~10 ft lower) as the true top, so most parties tag both. The upper 100-150 ft is loose broken rock but not technically difficult; no rope is normally needed.
Begins with low-angle scrambling over a block, then ascends steeper terrain to midpoint anchors; a bulge presents a crux on lichen-covered rock before easier terrain leads to the top.

A mildly overhanging start holds what is likely the pumpiest move of the climb low down, leading into numerous stemming moves up a crack system. A muddy ledge partway up (partially cleaned/"excavated" by early ascentionists, hence the name) breaks the climbing before a thinner, well-protected finishing crack. Currently top-roped off a static line anchored to a tree at the top; bolted anchors are planned but not yet installed.

EZ Way is a 5.6 trad climb on Shark Rock's west face. The rock is very solid but protection is extremely difficult due to minute cracks. A classic but serious alpine rock route requiring competent trad climbing skills and protection placement in difficult crack systems.
A few jugs and a fist jam get you through the crux to a bolted anchor shared with Bachelor Party.

Fifth of July Mountain's easiest route is straightforward class 2 hiking/scrambling up its south ridge — no rope or technical gear is needed for the peak itself. One approach starts at the Basalt Pass Trailhead, following the Basalt Ridge crest north past Point 6351 and a saddle below Devils Smoke Stack (a separate, harder class 3 summit), then dropping into a basin and climbing boulder fields and a larch-dotted bench to the peak's south ridge and summit. The longer approach, the one this route plan follows, comes from the Entiat River Trailhead via Myrtle Lake, Larch Lakes, and Cow Creek Pass, climbing the same south ridge from the east. Tread fades to nothing above treeline on both approaches, and route-finding across slick pumice and burned terrain (2020 Chikamin Creek Fire) is part of the challenge.

1,100 ft (333 m) of technical rock across 8 pitches, plus roughly 500 ft of 3rd-class scrambling to the summit. Climbs wild knobs and diorite fins reminiscent of California granite. Pitches are steep, long, and relatively sustained for alpine climbing; rock quality is generally very good but can be lichen-y/dirty in places from low traffic. Generally very good protection, especially at the cruxes, with a couple of runout sections (pitches 2 and 5).
Begins with an overhanging section, then eases up with a great resting point before the chain anchor.

Opens with a 100-foot 5.4 chimney and hand crack, then follows hands-and-fists and finger-crack corners (5.8-5.9) through a choss-cave belay, before a 5.10+ series of corners and roofs taking thin protection (knifeblades/Lost Arrows useful); the 5.11a crux comes right off a belay in super-thin cracks, after which easier pitches join Spontaneity Arete's ridge to the summit. Route lacks a fully sustained or continuously natural line, with some dirty/vegetated cracks in places.

Established by Darin Berdinka on September 11, 2017. Climbs a friction slab past 5 bolts, an easier bolted slab with a fixed pin, a long protectable seam pitch mixing gear and bolts, a short bolted connector pitch, and a final progressively harder face pitch to the top. Rock quality on this part of the face is generally excellent; pitches 1/2 and 3/4 can be readily linked with a 60m rope.

One of the best remote alpine rock routes in the North Cascades (listed among the 15 best routes in the Cascades). Mostly sustained ~5.9 climbing with brief 5.10 cruxes on Pitches 3 and 6; 34 protection bolts total and bolted belay anchors up to Pitch 7. Pitch 6 is the main crux, face climbing up a green-tinted slab; Pitch 7 tops out at 'Falcon's Perch,' an exposed viewpoint. Pairs well with Roan Wall - Center Stage for a big alpine linkup day for fast parties.
